# The canonical witness — faith alone, from the texts all parties accept

The sola fide argument works through the disputes that surround the doctrine:
what "works of the law" (ἔργα νόμου) denotes, whether "the faith of Christ"
(πίστις Χριστοῦ) is our faith in him, what "saved" (σῴζω) means at Luke 7:50.
This argument asks a narrower question, one those disputes can bury. Grant only
the texts that Rome and the Reformers both hold as Scripture. What does each
part of the New Testament say about how a person is justified, and does faith
alone follow?

Every text is a premise cited to Scripture alone. Romans, Galatians, Ephesians
and Titus are read together as Paul, whoever wrote the last two, because every
party receives them as canon and the question is what the canon says. Hebrews
is read as a corpus of its own, because it is anonymous. Trent grants all of
them, and its Decree on Justification quotes most. So the texts are rated
`consensus`, the highest rating, and nothing turns on them.

The argument is made in the readings. Each part of the New Testament is read in
one step, from its texts to what they say. That step is the reading, and it is
cited and rated, because texts do not entail conclusions and readings do. Each
corpus is made to deliver only what its own texts say, and *faith alone* is
split into three parts, so that no corpus has to carry more than its share:

- that faith is **necessary**: Paul ("not justified by works of the law except
  through faith", Galatians 2:16; "the righteous shall live by faith", 3:11),
  Hebrews ("without faith it is impossible to please God") and John ("whoever
  does not believe is condemned already");
- that faith is **sufficient**: Paul ("to the one who does not work but
  believes", Romans 4:5), John, Peter and Jesus' words in Luke;
- that works are **not the ground** of justification: Paul (Romans 3:28,
  Ephesians 2:9, Titus 3:5), Peter at the Jerusalem council, and Jesus' parable
  of the Pharisee and the tax collector.

The rival is Trent, which holds every one of these texts. Set beside the
canonical witness with James, it parts at exactly one reading: that "justified"
in James 2:24 is the *increase* of a justification already received, by works
done in grace (Session VI, ch. 10).

## What the early church said

The readings are cited to the Reformers and to modern exegetes. They are also
cited to fathers whom Rome itself venerates and cites, to show that the claims
Trent condemns were not coined in the sixteenth century.

- Clement of Rome: "not justified by ourselves … nor by works which we have
  wrought in holiness of heart; but by that faith through which, from the
  beginning, Almighty God has justified all men" (1 Clement 32.4).
- Polycarp: "by grace you are saved, not of works" (*Philippians* 1).
- The Epistle to Diognetus, which the Catechism cites (CCC 2271): "that the
  righteousness of One should justify many transgressors" (9).
- Hilary of Poitiers, a Doctor of the Church: "faith alone justifies", *fides
  enim sola iustificat* (*Commentary on Matthew* 8.6).
- Basil the Great, another: "to be justified by faith in Christ alone" (Homily
  20, *Of Humility*).

They show that faith's sufficiency, and the exclusion of works as ground, were
early Christian claims. They do not show that the fathers held the Reformers'
*forensic* account of what justification is, a declaring righteous rather than
a making righteous. Augustine reads justification as a making righteous, and
Trent follows him there. Chrysostom's seventh homily on Romans, on 3:27–28,
speaks of justification by faith without saying "faith alone". So the fathers
are cited for what they say, and the account of what justification is is
argued from Paul.

## What this does not show

It does not show that the Reformed readings are right. It shows where the
disagreement is. Every text is common ground, every reading is cited to the
people who hold it, and the results name, corpus by corpus, which readings a
reader must reject to deny the conclusion.

## The questions the later chapters take

- **What does each corpus say, and how is it read?** Each corpus's texts and its
  one reading, with the ratings ([What each corpus says](canonical-witness/the-readings.md)).
- **What must an opponent reject, and does James contradict Paul?** No single
  corpus carries the case, and there are exactly three ways to overturn it.
  James coheres with Paul on one reading of 2:14, and Trent parts at one
  reading of 2:24
  ([What follows, and what an opponent must reject](canonical-witness/the-burden.md)).
